text: A priest in a river village says the Flame went out for a heartbeat during the king's last hour.
Grain carts are arriving late. The drivers blame the roads and look at the soldiers.
Someone is selling 'the king's true will' in three different handwritings.
Varos merchants are asking, politely, who will honour Erol's border.
A company of unpaid spears was seen eating a lord's orchard.
The west says Harrow will kneel to anyone who is not Storm.
Sailors claim Celene Veyne already knows the winner and is only waiting to be paid for the knowledge.
Children in Caerlyn are playing four crowns and a knife.
An old sergeant drank to Ethan and was not arrested, which is its own news.
The eastern forts are counting Varos fires at night and pretending they are shepherds.
A Maren horse-trader says the vale is feeding more soldiers than it admits.
People who saw the covered bier disagree about whether the body was the king's height.
At the ferry below Caerlyn, a child has tied four scraps of cloth to the same reed. The boatman refuses to choose a colour.
The castle laundries have returned the black mourning cloth. No one has agreed what colour comes after it.
A cooper in Larkspool refuses a military contract until the buyer writes down who will pay if the king changes.
The fish market keeps the first catch for widows whose men are on the road. The second catch is sold to those men's captains.
Riders at Maren are arguing about the price of oats. They agree that horses have no interest in the succession.
An inn on the western road accepts flour in payment. It turns away banners that demand a room for nothing.
Caerlyn's printers have scraped another claimant's name off a proclamation block. The old letters still show in wet ink.
The bell-founders keep a spare crown candle beside the forge. They say a kingdom should always expect repairs.
A notary in the Riverlands charges the same fee to all four households. His apprentices are learning to write quickly.
The first snow reaches the northern watchposts. Men who argue about heirs share the same fire.
The masons have covered their unfinished work before the frost. The stones can wait; the wages cannot.
Harrow longbow makers now stamp the village as well as the lord's name on their bows. A weapon has more than one maker.
A river pilot has painted the safe depth marks twice, once for merchants and once for soldiers who cannot read.
The Temple Quarter has begun keeping a second register of the dead. Names arrive faster than the official messengers.
Wedding contracts in the south now include an escape clause for a second siege. The notaries call this prudence.
Flour costs less at the capital gates this week. Bakers leave their shutters open after dusk.
The northern roads are carrying carts as well as companies. There is room to step aside without being ordered.
A schoolmaster has resumed lessons interrupted by the succession. His pupils have learned more heraldry than he intended.
Merchants are offering contracts that run beyond the coronation. Confidence is beginning to appear in the small print.
The guard at the eastern tollhouse finds Varosi coin sewn into a grain sack. It buys the carrier a hearing, not a road.
At the Queen's new witness office, a carter corrects a clerk's arithmetic and lives to be proved right.
A midwife in the lower city has crossed out the word noble on a requisition. The same clean linen serves every mother.
The royal granary posts its receipts at eye level. Neighbours argue over the figures instead of over whose cousin has the key.
The palace inquest remains open to another petition. A kitchen servant has come with a name instead of a rumour.
At a roadside pension office, a veteran counts the payment twice, then buys boots for his daughter.
The new wardens escort a market cart without collecting a private toll. People are beginning to recognise their old regimental badges.
A veteran has reached the end of his service term. His captain signs the discharge rather than inventing another emergency.
A shelter clerk returns a list of names to the families who wrote it. No recruiter keeps a copy.
At Maren's sluice, the chalk marks show when the smaller fields are owed their water. Someone has left fresh bread for the keeper.
The vale has set aside grain for seed before anyone calculates a profit. Even the poorest tenants are discussing next year.
An apprentice at Lysa's workshop carries a new pair of shoes home. Her master knows whose savings made them possible.
A stable ledger bears Arlo's own signature beneath a disputed wage. He has paid it before asking anyone to call him royal.
The Storm mines post the names of the shift inspectors. A worker points out a bad brace before the bell sends anyone underground.
A northern widow reads the mine's compensation notice aloud. This time the promised sum is on the table beside it.
A southern magistrate rules against a northern officer and keeps her chair. The compact has survived its first serious test.
Storm's quartermasters have marked the reserve stores paid. The men know they will not have to collect their wages from a village.
The bargemen honour a delivery whose first cargo was lost. They remember who paid the widows without arguing over the seal.
A guild cart carries tools instead of levies. The apprentices beside it are arguing about their first wages.
At the shared infirmary, the cots are numbered. The banners have been left at the door.
Prisoners under the sowing truce return the borrowed ploughs. The repaired handles show which ones were used.
A parole clerk closes a case because the man came back when he said he would. Keeping a promise has become news.
Nessa Grey has signed a lease in her own name. The neighbours know her as the woman who pays on time.
The relief grain arrives under the same seals as the tax carts. At last the villages have seen those wagons coming both ways.
The Council has sent fresh copies of the final summons. Innkeepers are reserving rooms for witnesses as well as lords.
The coronation tailors ask for payment before cutting the cloth. They have fitted too many futures on credit.
A Riverlands family buries its winter seed in a sealed jar. The new ruler will have to earn the right to open it.
